chunks: "The core difference is that a brushed motor commutates mechanically with brushes riding on a commutator, and a brushless one commutates electronically with transistors.
Almost every advantage follows from getting rid of that sliding contact. First, lifetime and reliability.
Brushes wear out, typically somewhere in the range of a few thousand hours depending on the motor, while a brushless motor only has bearings to wear. Second, efficiency.
There's no brush friction and no brush voltage drop, which on a 12 volts motor can be around a volt, so roughly 8 percent of the input power, and much more on a 3 volts motor.
Third, electrical and acoustic noise. Brushes arc and generate broadband EMI and audible noise, and I need extra filtering.
A brushless motor can still be noisy, but the noise comes from PWM switching, which I control. Fourth, speed and power density.
Brushes limit top speed through bounce and wear, and the rotor winding is hard to cool because it's spinning in the middle.
In a BLDC the windings are on the stator, directly against the housing, so I can push more continuous current.
And there's no commutator spark, so it's safer in flammable environments. The trade-off is cost and complexity.
A brushed motor runs from a battery and a transistor, whereas a BLDC needs a three-phase bridge, position sensing and firmware.
For a cheap toy or a low-duty-cycle actuator, I'd still choose brushed."
